headline: AI robot company melts its old fleet in 75-ton vat of molten steel, Terminator-style
summary: Robotics firm Figure decommissioned its F.02 AI robots in a molten steel furnace to protect proprietary technology and make space for newer models. The dramatic send-off was inspired by a suggestion from Arnold Schwarzenegger.
details: Figure, a U.S.-based robotics company, decommissioned its F.02 AI robots by making them jump into a 75-ton furnace full of molten steel. The company stated that maintaining its F.02 fleet no longer made sense as its next-generation F.03 is increasing in numbers.

Disassembling the older robots was deemed difficult and time-consuming due to proprietary technology, and assigning an internal team would divert resources from the F.04 model. CEO Brett Adcock sought ideas on X for a "proper sendoff," receiving an unexpected reply from Arnold Schwarzenegger: "You should melt them."

This led to an "epic journey" of training robots to jump from a second story onto an airbag and finding a foundry willing to accept robots with lithium batteries. They eventually found a site in Finland that provided 24 hours and six melts for the process.

The decommissioning spectacle was a complete success, with the F.02 AI robots functioning as intended up to the last moment. This occurred despite the extreme heat and electromagnetic fields generated by the molten steel and high-voltage electricity.

The resulting metal bars were taken back to the U.S. and machined into limited-edition memorabilia commemorating the F.02. Most of the F.02 fleet has now been melted down and recycled, with only a few remaining in storage.

This process gives Figure more space for newer robot models and prevents proprietary technology from falling into the hands of competitors. One F.02 robot was even filmed holding a thumbs-up sign as it sank into the molten metal, creating a real-life Terminator-style ending.
caption:

headline_marked: [[ChatGPT-6 Astra cracks 217-year-old Napoleonic code]] in just six hours
headline: ChatGPT-6 Astra cracks 217-year-old Napoleonic code in just six hours
summary: OpenAI's model deciphered a message from Napoleon's stepson's headquarters, previously unsolved for decades, using only a single image and prompt.
details: GPT-6 Astra cracked a 217-year-old Napoleonic cipher in just six hours, a message that had remained unsolved on Cryptiana's Unsolved Historical Ciphers list for decades. It achieved this feat after being fed only a single image and prompt.

The cipher, from Eugène de Beauharnais' (Napoleon's stepson) headquarters, was a troop briefing sent to French General Auguste de Marmont. It relays Napoleon's orders regarding preparation for the Austrian invasion.

Engineer Carter Church of cybersecurity company SentinelOne used Astra for this breakthrough, noting the impressive multi-modal workflow. The freshly deciphered text even fills in some missing context from Napoleon’s 1865 memoir.

The encoded letter began with a plain text introductory line, followed by 24 rows of numbers, letters, and invented symbols. Astra utilized a partial key and its simulated-annealing solver to reveal the 19th-century military secret.

The solution's veracity is confirmed by Satoshi Tomokiyo, who maintains Cryptiana's online database, marking the letter as solved. Church also states the solution is "mechanically testable" against the ciphertext via a published solution package.
